# From case to slide deck [8 min]{.time} {#case-to-deck}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can run the four-step flow on Case A, take identifiers out before the first paste, and check an outline against the card.

**Have ready.** Your own assistant, signed in, in a window you can share, to run each step as the group does. The `case-outline` prompt, Case A and the teaching points are on the slides: click Copy prompt and paste each into the chat. One saved run as a backup.

**Clock.** 0:00 four steps. 1:00 identifiers out. 2:30 the prompt. 3:00 Case A. 3:30 teaching points, run it, tick every number. 6:00 read it against the card. 8:00 time.

**Watch for.** An outline that gains a learning objective, guideline or medicine the card does not contain. The outline treated as finished: it is step 2 of 4. A promised time saving: give no number: the site has none, and Lab One compared drafts, not minutes. A real case pasted "just this once": the privacy line, then the card.

**If asked.** A real patient's scan on a slide? An image can identify even with the caption removed; your institution's consent and image policy decides, so ask its data protection officer or legal team. I cannot give legal advice. The name is removed, so is it de-identified? That is one step; rare details can still point to one person, so when in doubt, use a card. Do I tell the audience AI helped? Follow your institution's or the meeting's policy.

**Bridge.** "An outline gives you the order. A talk needs the words, a line to say and a picture for each slide."
:::

## Four steps, two owners {#four-steps}

::: {.lane}
[1 · Case notes: yours, de-identified]{.node .dark .grow} [→]{.op} [2 · Outline: AI drafts, you check]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [3 · Slide draft: text, notes, visual idea]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [4 · Edit and delivery: yours]{.node .dark .grow}
:::

[▲ Dark boxes are yours. The light ones are the tool's draft, and you check them.]{.pointer}

Whatever you paste at step 1 is inherited by every step after it.

::: notes
**1:00.** Four steps, two owners. The dark boxes, steps 1 and 4, are yours: the case notes, de-identified, and the edit and delivery. The light boxes, steps 2 and 3, are the tool's draft, which you check: the outline, then the slide text. Whatever you paste at step 1 is inherited by everything after it, so step 1 is where identifiers come out. The handout says every step after the outline is faster with AI. Whether it is faster for you is yours to judge, so promise no saving.

**Do.** No move here. Say it once and go on.
:::

## Take identifiers out first {#deidentify-slides}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Text]{.t}

No name, file number, ID, phone or exact date.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[Images]{.t}

No scan, ECG or screenshot with a name on it.
:::
::: {.card}
[Combinations]{.t}

Rare details together can still point to one person. When in doubt, use a card.
:::
:::

> **No patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool. Ever. Full stop.**

::: notes
**1:30.** The privacy line, once more, word for word: no patient identifiers into a consumer AI tool, ever, full stop. For a teaching slide it covers two things: the prompt that builds the slide, and the slide itself. Leave out names and initials; file, ID and phone numbers; dates of birth and exact dates, so write six weeks ago, not the calendar date. Images need more care than text: a face, a tattoo or a distinctive scar identifies someone even with the caption removed, and a scan or ECG may carry a name in the corner. Rare details together can still point to one person; when in doubt, use a card. Your institution's policy on teaching material comes first. Day Three returns to this.

**Do.** Read the line aloud and pause for three seconds. No move here.
:::

## Read it against the card {#read-outline}

::: {.lane .sm}
[Invented]{.node .red .grow} [Card: nothing there]{.node .ghost .grow} [→]{.op} [Outline: a new fact]{.node .red .grow}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[Omitted]{.node .grow} [Card: a fact]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Outline: nothing there]{.node .ghost .grow}
:::
::: {.lane .sm}
[Altered]{.node .change .grow} [Card: a value, dose, side or unit]{.node .same .grow} [→]{.op} [Outline: a different one]{.node .change .grow}
:::

[▲ Omitted is fine if you chose it. It is a problem when the tool chose it and the talk depends on it.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} Type one thing your outline left out, and whether you would have left it out too.
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** Read the outline against the card for the three ways drafted clinical text goes wrong: invented, omitted, altered. Omission is fine when you chose it. It becomes a problem when the tool chose it and the talk depends on it. On Case A the father's stroke is a candidate: only you know whether a slide about follow-up needs it. Fix the outline by hand, or tell the tool exactly what to change, before building on it: an error left here is copied onto every slide.

**Do.** Chat for one minute. Read out two or three answers and sort each aloud as invented, omitted or altered. Leave them with the line: take identifiers out first, check the outline against your notes, and keep the final edit for yourself. Then the bridge from the topic slide.
:::

# Building a full talk, not just an outline [12 min]{.time} {#full-talk}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can turn an approved outline into slide text, one speaker note and one visual idea per slide, and check the result before anyone else sees it.

**Have ready.** Case A, the approved three-slide outline from the last topic, and the `full-talk-slides` prompt in your assistant, with a saved run as a backup. The handout's illustrative output in a window of your own, to show the VISUAL line for slide 2.

**Clock.** 0:00 three things per slide. 1:15 the ledger. 1:45 run it. 5:00 a picture is a suggestion. 7:45 slide check. 10:45 one slide at a time. 11:30 "more convincing". 12:00 time.

**Watch for.** A visual suggestion treated as data: if a tool draws a line of daily readings, every point on it is made-up. Slide text that grows past three lines, or a statistic nobody asked for. The ledger treated as proof: tick against the card. Asking for the whole deck again: it can change slides you already checked.

**If asked.** Can it draw the actual chart? Some tools can; the values still come from you and the source, so check every axis and label. Can it add references? It can produce ones that look real and are not; a citation you did not open is not a citation, so delete it or find the original yourself. Can I paste a colleague's slides or a published figure? Only material you are allowed to share with a third-party tool; ask your institution.

**Bridge.** "You have been the presenter. Now the teacher: the same tool writes quiz questions, with one habit worth knowing."
:::

## One level past the outline {#three-things}

::: {.lane}
[One slide of your approved outline]{.node .same .grow}
:::

::: {.fan}
[▼]{.a} [▼]{.a} [▼]{.a}
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[01]{.num}

**Slide text.** A title and at most three short lines.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[02]{.num}

**Speaker note.** One line to say.
:::
::: {.card}
[03]{.num}

**Visual.** What to show, not the picture.
:::
:::

[▲ Ask for these three and nothing more. Every extra line becomes yours to verify.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:15.** The outline gave you the order. The hours go into the words on each slide, what you will say, and the picture, and that is where a tool has the most room to add things you did not ask for. So ask for exactly three things per slide: the slide text, one line of speaker notes, and one visual suggestion. The short list is the discipline. Ask for a full slide and you may get paragraphs, a supporting statistic and a source line, and all three become yours to verify. Ask for three things and you have three things to check.

**Do.** No move here. Keep it to seventy-five seconds.
:::

## A picture is a suggestion, not data {#visual-trap}

::: {.lane}
[Case A gives one home number: average 146/92, last 2 weeks, mornings]{.node .teal .grow} [→]{.op} [A chart with a point for every day]{.node .change .grow}
:::

::: {.lane .sm}
[Daily readings: not on the card]{.node .ghost .grow} [→]{.op} [Every point on the chart would be made-up]{.node .red .grow}
:::

[▲ The numbers in a chart come from you and the source, never from the tool.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} Look at the VISUAL line for the diary slide. Does it ask for daily readings? Type yes or no.
:::

::: notes
**2:45.** Here is the trap. A visual suggestion is a suggestion. If a tool proposes a chart of the home blood pressure diary, ask which points it would plot. Case A gives only the two-week average, so any daily value on that chart would be made-up. The numbers in a chart come from you and the source, never from the tool: AI drafts. You decide. On the handout's illustrative output, the VISUAL line for slide 2 says no daily values: that is the constraint working.

**Do.** Chat, yes or no, then read out two or three VISUAL lines. If one asks for daily readings, ask what to do next: delete it, or ask for a table of the average beside the clinic readings.
:::

## Slide check, once per slide {#slide-qa}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Numbers]{.t}

[]{.chk} Every number and chart value matches the source.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[Identifiers]{.t}

[]{.chk} None on the slide or in the image.
:::
::: {.card}
[Claims]{.t}

[]{.chk} Each one sourced. One idea per slide.
:::
:::

[▲ Three ticks for each slide, before anyone else sees it.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .share}
[Share · 3 min]{.tag} A volunteer shares a screen with their three slides. Everyone types one finding: a mismatch, something not on the card, or "clean".
:::

::: notes
**3:00.** Run this once per slide, before anyone else sees it. Numbers: digit by digit, value, unit, side, and which reading it belongs to; tick against the card, not against the tool's ledger. Identifiers: no name, file number, exact date, or image that shows a face or a name. Claims: each has a source you can name or is your own statement; delete any citation, statistic or guideline the tool added. One idea per slide, three lines at most.

**Do.** Share. Ask for one volunteer to share their three slides; if nobody offers, share your own saved run and check it aloud. Everyone types one finding. Read out three, then ask which was the riskiest.
:::

# Teaching with AI [8 min]{.time} {#teaching-with-ai}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can get quiz questions from a source they may share, and check whether the correct answers are balanced by position and length.

**Have ready.** The `quiz-from-source` prompt and the practice source are on the slides: click Copy prompt and paste each into the chat. A saved run as a backup. Everyone keeps their own quiz open: the next topic uses it.

**Clock.** 0:00 three uses. 0:45 only from this text. 1:45 the prompt. 2:15 the source, run it. 4:45 check the letters and the lengths. 7:00 the fix. 8:00 time.

**Watch for.** The prompt already asks for balance, so a live run may pass: check anyway, and if it balanced, say so and do not manufacture a failure. A rewrite that fixes the letters but changes a fact. A trainee pasting a real note "just to tidy it": the privacy line. Questions asked for from general memory: a wrong question reads exactly like a right one.

**If asked.** Can I paste a paper or guideline? Only if you may share it with a third-party tool; its terms and your institution's policy decide, and if you do not know, do not paste. I cannot give legal advice. Can it mark my residents' answers? It can draft feedback against a rubric you supply; you decide the grade and what the trainee hears. Are these good enough for a real exam? They are first drafts; the next topic covers the key.

**Bridge.** "The questions are checked against the source. The key is the part people forget, because a wrong key looks like an authority."
:::

## Three uses {#teaching-ai}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Quiz questions]{.t}

From a source you may share, checked against it.
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[Study summaries]{.t}

A fixed shape and a word limit, as with a note.
:::
::: {.card}
[Supervising]{.t}

Ask for the prompt and the source, then check together.
:::
:::

You practice summaries in Lab 2, part 2.

::: notes
**0:45.** Three uses, one line each. Quiz questions written only from a source you paste, then checked against it. Study summaries with the same discipline as a note: a fixed shape, a word limit, numbers copied exactly, and you read every line before a trainee does. Supervising: when a trainee brings an AI draft, ask to see the prompt and the source, then run the three-question check on it together. Say the privacy line to trainees too: a trainee in a hurry may paste a real note just to tidy it.

**Do.** No move here. Keep it to forty-five seconds.
:::

## The habit to check {#mcq-habit}

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .dashed}
[ANSWER LETTERS]{.t}

[1-C]{.pill .red} [2-C]{.pill .red} [3-C]{.pill .red} [4-B]{.pill} [5-C]{.pill .red}

Does one letter carry most of the answers?
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[Question 2: how long is each option?]{.t}

::: {.nextword}
::: {.row}
[A]{.w} []{.fill style="width:5.3em"}
:::
::: {.row}
[B]{.w} []{.fill style="width:5.8em"}
:::
::: {.row}
[C]{.w} []{.fill .flat style="width:12em"}
:::
::: {.row}
[D]{.w} []{.fill style="width:4.5em"}
:::
:::

Is the correct option the longest?
:::
:::

[▲ Four of five answers are C, and in question 2 the correct option (teal) is also the longest.]{.pointer}

[Illustrative, written for this course]{.illustrative}

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} Type your ANSWER LETTERS, then balanced or not.
:::

::: notes
**2:15.** A real weakness to check for. Tools that write multiple-choice questions tend to put the correct answer in the same position, and to make it the longest option. Both let a learner pass by guessing a letter or picking the longest option, without reading the source. The prompt already asks for balance, so check that it happened: read ANSWER LETTERS, then find the longest option in each question. The example on the slide is unbalanced on purpose, written for this course.

**Do.** Chat: everyone types their letters, then balanced or not. Read out two or three. If a run balanced, say so; do not manufacture a failure.
:::

## Ask for the fix in plain words {#plain-words-fix}

::: {.lane}
[A check fails]{.node .red} [→]{.op} [Reply in the same chat: which questions, what is wrong, what you want]{.node .change .grow} [→]{.op} [Check the new quiz against the source again]{.node .teal .grow}
:::

{{< include _paste-m5-quiz-fix.md >}}

[▲ Copy prompt on your slide. Fill in the brackets from your own quiz. A rewrite can change a fact.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 1 min]{.tag} If a check failed, fill the brackets and send it. If your quiz balanced, leave it.
:::

::: notes
**1:00.** If either check fails, reply in the same chat, in plain words: say which questions, say what is wrong, say what you want. Then check the rewritten questions against the source again, because a rewrite can change a fact; fixing the letters while changing a number is a bad trade. If your quiz already balanced, say so and do not manufacture a failure. The questions are checked against the source. The key is the part people forget, because a wrong key looks like an authority.

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too. Read the reply aloud. Leave them with the line: paste the source and say only from this text, then check whether the answer positions and lengths are balanced; do not assume they are. Then the bridge from the topic slide.
:::

# Grading yourself [7 min]{.time} {#grading-yourself}

::: notes
**Goal.** Everyone can ask for an answer key with a quotation for every answer, and spot-check the riskiest line against the real source.

**Have ready.** The quiz from the last topic open, and the practice source as you pasted it in the chat, to point at when you reach line 6. The `answer-key-with-quotes` prompt is on a slide: click Copy prompt and paste it into the chat.

**Clock.** 0:00 grade the key. 1:00 ask for quotations, run it, check the riskiest line. 3:30 key versus source. 5:30 the same check. 7:00 time.

**Watch for.** Checking the tool's copy of the source, or its quotation, instead of the real source. "It passed, so the rest is fine": a pass verifies one line, and the quotations only make the others quick to check. A quotation that is nearly right: shortened, or one word changed. Running long: the spot-check is the point, the discussion is optional.

**If asked.** Isn't it enough to check everything? If you have time, yes; the spot-check is the minimum, and it says what to do when the minimum fails. How can a quotation be wrong if it came from the source? It can be shortened, altered or from the wrong line. Can a second tool check the first one's key? It can point you at lines to look at; agreement between two tools is not a source. What if the source itself is wrong? Then the key is faithful to a wrong source; check against the guideline or label you trust.

**Bridge.** "That is Day Two's toolkit: notes, three audiences, talks and teaching. After the break, Lab Two puts it together: one case, three outputs."
:::

## Grade the key before it grades anyone {#grade-yourself}

A wrong key marks the right trainee wrong, in the same confident voice as a right one.

::: {.lane}
[Practice source]{.node .same .fixed} [→]{.op} [Your quiz]{.node .out .grow} [→]{.op} [Key: a quotation for every answer]{.node .change .grow} [→]{.op} [You check it against the source]{.node .teal .grow}
:::

Checked line by line: &emsp; []{.chk} 1 &emsp; []{.chk} 2 &emsp; []{.chk} 3 &emsp; []{.chk} 4 &emsp; []{.chk} 5

[▲ Riskiest first: a number, an exception, a threshold or a negation. If it fails, the rest is unchecked, not fine.]{.pointer}

::: notes
**1:00.** A quiz is an assessment. If its key is wrong, a trainee who answered correctly is marked wrong. The tool writes a wrong key line in the same confident voice as a right one, so "does this look right" is not a test. Ask for the key in the same conversation as the questions, with a quotation for every answer. Then check the riskiest question first: the one with a number, an exception, a threshold or a negation. If that check fails, the rest is unchecked, not fine.

**Do.** No move here. One minute.
:::

## Ask for a quotation with every answer {#ask-for-quotes}

::: {.lane .sm}
[The letter]{.node .same .grow} [+]{.op} [The exact words, in quotation marks]{.node .teal .grow} [+]{.op} [The line they come from]{.node .same .grow}
:::

::: {.paste-long}
{{< include _paste-answer-key-with-quotes.md >}}
:::

[▲ Copy prompt on your slide. The same chat as your quiz, so it is the same quiz.]{.pointer}

::: {.move .solo}
[Solo · 2 min]{.tag} Run it. Check your riskiest question's quotation against the practice source in the chat.
:::

::: notes
**2:30.** Run it in the same conversation as the questions, so it is the same quiz. For each answer you get the letter, the exact words from the source inside quotation marks, and the line or heading they come from. A quotation turns "is this answer right" into "does this line say that", which you settle with the source in front of you. If no words support an answer, the prompt makes the tool write NOT SUPPORTED instead. Riskiest means a trap: a number, an exception, a threshold or a negation.

**Do.** Tell them to click Copy prompt on their slide, and paste the block into the chat too. Run it on the shared screen while the group runs it on theirs: solo for two minutes, then check the riskiest quotation against the practice source in the chat. Then Chat: pass or fail? If the clock is short, cut the second minute; the spot-check is the point.
:::

## Key versus source {#key-vs-source}

::: {.lane}
[The key says, question 3: A, all readings from days 1 to 7. "Average all readings."]{.node .red .grow} [≠]{.op .fragment data-fragment-index="1"} [The source says, line 6: "Discard the readings from day 1. Average all remaining readings."]{.node .teal .grow .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
:::

[Illustrative: the key is written for this course]{.illustrative}

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
[]{.chk .no} The quotation is in line 6, word for word.

[]{.chk .on} It says what the key claims.

[]{.chk .no} The line supports the letter in the key.
:::

::: {.move .chat}
[Chat · 1 min]{.tag} Is the key's quotation in line 6, word for word? Type yes or no.
:::

::: notes
**2:00.** The spot-check, on an illustrative key written for this course. Three things to check on the riskiest line: the quotation appears word for word, it says what the key claims, and it supports the letter given. Question 3 asks which readings are averaged. The key says all readings from days 1 to 7, quoting "Average all readings." The real source, line 6, reads "Discard the readings from day 1. Average all remaining readings." The quotation is not there: it is shortened and drops the discard, and the key's answer follows it. If it fails, the rest is unchecked; if it passes, one line is verified.

**Do.** Show the practice source you pasted, so line 6 is in view. Chat: yes or no. Click to show line 6, then the three checks. Ask what to do with the other questions: check each, or discard the set.
:::

## The same check, in your words {#same-check}

::: {.lane .sm}
[Draft with AI: the key]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [Cross-check the source]{.node .teal .grow} [→]{.op} [Confirm or correct]{.node .grow} [→]{.op} [Use]{.node .dark .grow}
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[1]{.num}

**Could I defend this to a colleague?**
:::
::: {.card .teal}
[2]{.num}

**Does it point to something I can verify?**
:::
::: {.card}
[3]{.num}

**Would I catch it if it were wrong?**
:::
:::

If the answer to any of these is no, that's the signal to slow down, not the finding to accept.

::: notes
**1:30.** This is the verification workflow: Draft with AI → Cross-check the source → Confirm or correct → Use. The key is the draft; the source is the cross-check. Then the three questions, word for word. The key line for question 3 fails the first one the moment a colleague opens line 6. The quotation is what makes the second answerable. You pass the third only by opening the source, which is why the spot-check is a required step. Then the no rule, word for word.

**Do.** Read the no rule aloud and pause. Leave them with the line: ask for a quotation with every answer and check the riskiest line first; if it fails, the rest is unchecked, not fine. Then the bridge from the topic slide.
:::
